questions.question: What does JWT stand for and what is its purpose?

options.text: Java Web Token - for Java applications only
JSON Web Token - a compact, self-contained token for securely transmitting information
JavaScript Web Transfer - for transferring JS code
JSON Wrapper Type - for wrapping JSON data

questions.explanation: JWT (JSON Web Token) is a standard (RFC 7519) for creating tokens that contain claims (user info, permissions). They're self-contained, meaning the server can validate them without database lookups.

questions.question: What are the three parts of a JWT?
questions.explanation: JWT has three Base64-encoded parts separated by dots: Header (algorithm, type), Payload (claims/data), Signature (verification). Format: xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz

questions.question: Why is the JWT signature important?

options.text: It proves the token hasn't been tampered with and was issued by a trusted source

questions.explanation: The signature is created using the header, payload, and a secret/private key. Servers verify the signature to ensure the token is authentic and unmodified. Note: signature provides integrity, not confidentiality.

questions.question: True or False: JWT payload data is encrypted and cannot be read without the secret key.
questions.explanation: JWT payload is Base64-encoded, NOT encrypted. Anyone can decode and read it. The signature only prevents tampering, not reading. Never put sensitive data in JWTs unless using JWE (encrypted JWTs).

questions.question: What is the 'exp' claim in a JWT?

options.text: The expiration time after which the token is invalid

questions.explanation: 'exp' (expiration) is a standard claim containing a Unix timestamp. Servers should reject tokens where current time > exp. This limits the window for stolen tokens to be misused.

questions.question: A JWT is stolen by an attacker. What can limit the damage?

options.text: Short expiration times and token refresh mechanisms

questions.explanation: Short-lived JWTs (minutes, not days) limit the attack window. Refresh tokens (stored securely, can be revoked) issue new JWTs. Token blacklisting can invalidate compromised tokens before expiry.

questions.question: What is the difference between symmetric (HS256) and asymmetric (RS256) JWT signing?

options.text: HS256 is faster, RS256 is slower
HS256 uses shared secret; RS256 uses public/private key pair

questions.explanation: HS256: same secret signs and verifies (simpler, secret must be shared). RS256: private key signs, public key verifies (better for distributed systems—verifiers don't need the signing secret).

questions.question: Where should JWTs be stored in a browser application?

options.text: HttpOnly cookies for security, or memory for SPAs (tradeoffs exist)

questions.explanation: HttpOnly cookies prevent XSS access but require CSRF protection. localStorage is accessible to JS (XSS risk). Memory is safest but lost on refresh. Each has tradeoffs; HttpOnly cookies are often recommended.

questions.question: What is a refresh token and how does it relate to JWTs?

options.text: A token that refreshes the page
A long-lived token used to obtain new short-lived JWTs without re-authentication
A token that updates user data

questions.explanation: Refresh tokens are long-lived, stored securely (HttpOnly cookie, server-side), and exchanged for new JWTs when they expire. They can be revoked server-side, unlike stateless JWTs.

questions.question: Which JWT claims are registered (standard) claims? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: Registered claims are predefined: iss (issuer), sub (subject), aud (audience), exp (expiration), nbf (not before), iat (issued at), jti (JWT ID). 'username' would be a custom/private claim.

questions.question: A microservices architecture uses JWTs for service-to-service authentication. What is an advantage of this approach?

options.text: Services must call an auth server for every request
Services can validate tokens locally without network calls
JWTs automatically encrypt all service communication

questions.explanation: JWTs are self-contained—services verify the signature locally using the public key or shared secret. No auth server roundtrip needed per request, reducing latency and auth server load.

questions.question: What is the 'none' algorithm vulnerability in JWT?

options.text: An attack where tokens with 'alg: none' bypass signature verification

questions.explanation: Some JWT libraries accepted 'alg: none' (no signature), allowing attackers to forge tokens. Servers must explicitly whitelist allowed algorithms and reject 'none'. This was a serious vulnerability in early implementations.
